content.text:
### Railway reverse proxy request headers (X-Real-IP, no X-Forwarded-For) Source: https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/main/content/docs/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits.md Documents the exact headers Railway's edge reverse proxy injects into requests to public services. The client's remote IP is sent via X-Real-IP, plus X-Forwarded-Proto (always https) and X-Forwarded-Host. Notably, X-Forwarded-For is NOT listed among the forwarded headers, so Fastify's trustProxy logic (which derives request.ip from X-Forwarded-For) won't find it; the client IP is available via the X-Real-IP header instead. The repo does not publish proxy IP ranges to trust, so Fastify should read X-Real-IP directly rather than trusting a specific proxy CIDR list. ```markdown | **Request Headers** | - `X-Real-IP` for identifying client's remote IP.
- `X-Forwarded-Proto` always indicates `https`.
- `X-Forwarded-Host` for identifying the original host header.
- `X-Railway-Edge` for identifying the edge [POP](https://status.railway.com/locations) that handled the request.
- `X-Request-Start` for identifying the time the request was received (Unix milliseconds timestamp).
- `X-Railway-Request-Id` for correlating requests against network logs.
- `X-Railway-Debug` can be sent by clients with any value to receive extra debug response headers, currently `X-Railway-Upstream-Zone` (the origin zone that served the request). | ``` -------------------------------- ### Specs & Limits > Technical specifications Source: https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/main/content/docs/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits.md | **Request Headers** | - `X-Real-IP` for identifying client's remote IP.
- `X-Forwarded-Proto` always indicates `https`.
- `X-Forwarded-Host` for identifying the original host header.
- `X-Railway-Edge` for identifying the edge [POP](https://status.railway.com/locations) that handled the request.
- `X-Request-Start` for identifying the time the request was received (Unix milliseconds timestamp).
- `X-Railway-Request-Id` for correlating requests against network logs.
- `X-Railway-Debug` can be sent by clients with any value to receive extra debug response headers, currently `X-Railway-Upstream-Zone` (the origin zone that served the request). | -------------------------------- ### Edge proxy terminates TLS and adds headers Source: https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/main/content/docs/networking/edge-networking.md Describes the request flow through Railway's public networking: the edge proxy (tcp-proxy) terminates TLS, adds headers, and looks up routing information before forwarding traffic to the deployment — confirming the headers are injected by the proxy layer. ```markdown 2. **Edge Processing**: The edge proxy (tcp-proxy) terminates TLS, adds headers, and looks up routing information 3. **Internal Routing**: Traffic is forwarded over Railway's internal network to your deployment 4. **Service Response**: Your service processes the request and the response follows the reverse path ```

content.text:
### Intermediate layers with uv sync --no-install-project

Source: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/docs/guides/integration/docker.md

Use uv sync --no-install-project to install dependencies without the project itself, improving build times by caching dependencies in a separate layer. Only uv.lock is mounted for the first sync; pyproject.toml and project contents are copied before the final uv sync.

```dockerfile
# Install uv
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest /uv /uvx /bin/

# Change the working directory to the `app` directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
    --mount=type=bind,source=uv.lock,target=uv.lock \
    uv sync --frozen --no-install-project

# Copy the project into the image
COPY . /app

# Sync the project
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
    uv sync --locked
```

--------------------------------

### Set UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE environment variable

Source: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/docs/guides/integration/docker.md

Set UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 to ensure all uv commands within the Dockerfile compile bytecode. Note that uv only compiles the standard library of managed Python versions during uv python install; unmanaged Python versions may not have a pre-compiled standard library.

```dockerfile
ENV UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1
```

--------------------------------

### Optimizations > Intermediate layers

Source: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/docs/guides/integration/docker.md

If you're using uv to manage your project, you can improve build times by moving your transitive
dependency installation into its own layer via the `--no-install` options.

`uv sync --no-install-project` will install the dependencies of the project but not the project
itself. Since the project changes frequently, but its dependencies are generally static, this can be
a big time saver.

--------------------------------

### Optimizations > Intermediate layers

Source: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/docs/guides/integration/docker.md

Note that only the `uv.lock` file is mounted for the first sync. The `pyproject.toml` and project
_contents_ are copied into the image before the final `uv sync` command.

--------------------------------

### Enable bytecode compilation with --compile-bytecode flag

Source: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/docs/guides/integration/docker.md

Use the --compile-bytecode flag with uv python install and uv sync to compile Python source files to bytecode, improving startup time at the cost of increased installation time and image size.

```dockerfile
RUN uv python install --compile-bytecode
RUN uv sync --compile-bytecode
```

# One long-lived service: API, chat page and (later) the alert scheduler in one process.
# Base: official Python 3.12 slim image; uv binary copied from its official image (pinned).
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.3 /uv /uvx /bin/

WORKDIR /app
ENV UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 \
    UV_LINK_MODE=copy \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH"

# Dependencies first, in their own layer, so code changes don't reinstall them.
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN uv sync --locked --no-dev --no-install-project

# Then the project itself (code, hub config, committed seed snapshot).
COPY . .
RUN uv sync --locked --no-dev

# Railway sets PORT; the CLI reads it. DATA_DIR (refreshed data, later SQLite) is set to the
# volume's mount path as a Railway variable, so it is not baked into the image.
CMD ["python", "-m", "weather_risk", "serve", "--host", "0.0.0.0"]

"""Smoke-check a running deployment: health, an LLM-free ranking, and one chat question.

Usage: python scripts/smoke_deploy.py https://<your-app>.up.railway.app
Prints a short summary and exits non-zero on the first failure.
"""

import sys

import httpx


def main(base: str) -> None:
    base = base.rstrip("/")
    with httpx.Client(timeout=90) as http:
        health = http.get(f"{base}/api/health")
        health.raise_for_status()
        print("health  ", health.status_code, health.json())

        ranks = http.get(f"{base}/api/rankings", params={"hazard": "winter", "region": "Midwest"})
        ranks.raise_for_status()
        rows = ranks.json()["rows"]
        print("rankings", ranks.status_code, [(r["rank"], r["hub_id"], r["score"]) for r in rows[:3]])

        chat = http.post(f"{base}/api/chat",
                         json={"message": "Which hubs in the Midwest are most exposed to winter disruption?"})
        chat.raise_for_status()
        answer = chat.json()["answer"]
        print("chat    ", chat.status_code, answer["answer_type"], "|", answer["narrative"][:200])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "http://localhost:8000")

## 2026-11-13 - Railway deployment (step 1, no spec)

- **Build: Dockerfile, not Railpack.** `python:3.12-slim` plus the pinned uv binary (0.13.3), dependencies in their own layer (`uv sync --locked --no-dev --no-install-project`), then the code and the committed seed. Alternative: Railpack, which auto-detects `uv.lock` with zero config. Rejected because its build steps are implicit, so they are harder to explain and cannot be reproduced locally; the Dockerfile was built and run locally with Docker before the first deploy.
- **Config as code:** `railway.toml` sets the Dockerfile builder, the healthcheck (`/api/health`) and the restart policy. Secrets and environment values (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `DATA_DIR`, `TRUSTED_IP_HEADER`) are Railway variables, never in the repo or the image (`.dockerignore` excludes `.env`).
- **Real client IPs for the rate limiter.** Railway's docs list `X-Real-IP` as the client-IP header and do not list `X-Forwarded-For`, which is the only header uvicorn's `forwarded_allow_ips` reads. Behind the proxy every request would otherwise share the proxy's IP, turning the per-client limit into one global limit. Chosen: a setting `TRUSTED_IP_HEADER` (unset locally, `X-Real-IP` on Railway); when set, the limiter keys on that header. Unset by default, because without a proxy in front a client could set the header itself to dodge the limit. Two smoke tests cover both cases. Alternative: `forwarded_allow_ips="*"`, rejected because it depends on a header Railway does not document.
- **Deploy route: GitHub repo connected in the Railway dashboard.** The Railway CLI was the first choice, but Windows Application Control blocks `railway.exe` on the development machine (the same block as `wra.exe`). The dashboard route also gives auto-deploy on every push to `main`.
- **Volume** mounted at `/data`, with `DATA_DIR=/data`. Nothing writes there yet except `wra refresh`; it exists for the alert feature's SQLite score history. Railway does not allow replicas with a volume, which matches the single-instance design (in-memory conversations and rate limits).
- **Local test quirk:** the development machine's antivirus (Avast Web/Mail Shield) re-signs TLS, so `uv sync` inside a local Docker build fails with `UnknownIssuer`. The local test used a scratch copy of the Dockerfile that trusts that root CA; the committed Dockerfile has no such workaround, because Railway's builders reach PyPI directly.
- **Deploy smoke check:** `python scripts/smoke_deploy.py <url>` checks health, an LLM-free ranking and one chat question.
EOF

The deploy config is committed and pushed to `main` (`21b2725`). Now the part only you can do, in the Railway dashboard. Please follow these steps in order:

1. Go to **railway.com → New Project → Deploy from GitHub repo**, and pick `Slaharog/weather-risk-agent`. If the repo isn't listed, click **Configure GitHub App** and grant Railway access to that private repo. Railway will find `railway.toml` and build from the Dockerfile.
2. The first build may start right away. Let it run, or cancel it. It can't pass the healthcheck usefully until the variables exist, but the app still starts without the key, so it may go green.
3. Open the service, go to the **Variables** tab, and add:
   - `OPENAI_API_KEY` = your key. Paste it yourself; don't send it to me.
   - `DATA_DIR` = `/data`
   - `TRUSTED_IP_HEADER` = `X-Real-IP`
4. Right-click the service on the canvas (or use the command palette) and choose **Attach Volume**, with mount path `/data`.
5. Go to **Settings → Networking → Generate Domain**. If it asks for a port, enter `8080`. Railway sets `PORT` itself, and the app reads it.
6. Click **Deploy** to apply the staged changes. Then paste the `*.up.railway.app` URL here.

**Spend limit:** please also set a monthly budget or hard limit on the OpenAI project that owns this key (platform.openai.com → your project → **Limits**). The app caps chat at 10 messages per minute per client and 500 per day, but the URL will be public, so the OpenAI-side limit is the real backstop.

Once you send the URL, I'll run `scripts/smoke_deploy.py` against it, check which IP headers actually arrive, and then start Spec 002.

# Feature Specification: Core Weather Risk Agent

**Feature Branch**: `001-core-risk-agent`

**Created**: 2026-11-13

**Status**: Approved (2026-11-13)

**Input**: User description: "Core weather risk agent: a fixed list of US distribution hubs with coordinates and regions; ingestion of public weather and hazard data with a committed seed snapshot of real API responses plus a refresh command; deterministic, decomposable per-hub risk scoring (weighted per-hazard components) and statistics such as percentage of snow days; an LLM agent (OpenAI, hand-written tool-calling loop, strict JSON schema final answer with data_sources, assumptions, limitations, confidence) that answers ranking, comparison, statistic, and "why" questions with conversational follow-ups; exposed through a FastAPI chat API used by a simple web chat page; plus a runnable eval set of 15-25 cases. Out of scope for this spec: scheduled risk-change alerts and voice input (separate specs)."

## User Scenarios & Testing *(mandatory)*

The primary user is a logistics **analyst** who must recommend which hubs get resilience investment this year. A secondary user is the **operator** (the developer or a reviewer) who runs the system, refreshes data, and checks its quality.

All analyst journeys happen in a chat conversation. Every answer has the same shape: a short narrative, a table of the relevant numbers, and an "about this answer" panel listing data sources and period, assumptions, limitations, and a confidence level.

### User Story 1 - Rank hubs by exposure (Priority: P1)

The analyst asks which hubs are most exposed to a hazard, optionally within a region, for example "Which hubs in the Midwest are most exposed to winter disruption?" The agent returns the matching hubs ranked by their score for that hazard, with each hub's score, the main contributing factors, and the reasoning.

**Why this priority**: ranking is the core decision the business wants support for: which hubs to invest in. On its own, this story is a usable product.

**Independent Test**: ask the Midwest winter question in the chat. Verify that only Midwest hubs appear, that they are ordered by winter score, and that the numbers equal the scoring output for those hubs.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** the hub list and data snapshot are loaded, **When** the analyst asks "Which hubs in the Midwest are most exposed to winter disruption?", **Then** the answer lists only Midwest hubs, ranked highest to lowest by winter score, with the score and top contributing factors for each.
2. **Given** the same setup, **When** the analyst asks for the overall most at-risk hubs with no region or hazard, **Then** all hubs are ranked by overall score and the answer states which hazards drive the top hubs.
3. **Given** a region with no hubs, **When** the analyst asks about it, **Then** the agent says no hubs exist in that region and lists the regions that do.

---

### User Story 2 - Explain why a hub's risk is high (Priority: P1)

The analyst asks "Why is the Dallas hub's weather disruption risk high?" The agent shows the hub's overall score broken into per-hazard components, identifies the largest contributors, and explains each one with the underlying observations (for example, number of extreme heat days or the hazard rating for its location). It also shows how the hub compares with the other hubs.

**Why this priority**: an investment recommendation has to be defensible. The analyst must be able to explain any score to management, and this is what makes the ranking trustworthy.

**Independent Test**: ask the Dallas question. Verify that the components shown add up to the overall score, that the hazards named as main drivers are the largest components, and that the underlying values match the data.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** the data is loaded, **When** the analyst asks why Dallas's risk is high, **Then** the answer shows every component of Dallas's overall score, the components sum to the overall score, and the narrative names the largest components as the drivers.
2. **Given** a hub whose risk is actually low relative to the others, **When** the analyst asks why it is high, **Then** the agent corrects the premise, states its actual position, and still shows the breakdown.

---

### User Story 3 - Compare hubs on chosen hazards (Priority: P2)

The analyst asks "Compare Miami and Houston in terms of hurricane and flood exposure." The agent returns a side-by-side comparison of the requested hazards for the requested hubs, states which hub is more exposed on each hazard, and explains the difference.

**Why this priority**: comparing shortlisted candidates is the next most common step after ranking.

**Independent Test**: ask the Miami/Houston question. Verify both hubs and both hazards appear, and that the "more exposed" verdict on each hazard matches the higher score.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** the data is loaded, **When** the analyst compares Miami and Houston on hurricane and flood, **Then** the answer shows both hubs' scores for both hazards and a per-hazard verdict consistent with the scores.
2. **Given** the analyst names a city that is not a hub, **When** asking for a comparison, **Then** the agent says that city is not a hub, lists the hubs in the same region when the region can be determined, and does not invent data.

# Feature Specification: Risk-Change Alert

**Feature Branch**: `002-risk-change-alert` (work happens on `main`; no branch hook is configured)

**Created**: 2026-11-13

**Status**: Draft

**Input**: User description: "Risk-change alert (bonus feature). A scheduled job recomputes every hub's risk scores and records them; when a hub's score changes by more than a threshold compared with the last recorded score, the system fires an alert. Alerts go to a webhook URL that comes only from configuration/environment (never from chat), are always logged, and are listed at GET /api/alerts. A manual trigger (CLI command and/or endpoint) runs the check on demand for demos. Because real data changes rarely, there must be a way to demonstrate a change (e.g. a demo command or test fixture). Score history persists across restarts (planned: SQLite on the Railway volume at DATA_DIR). The scheduler runs inside the single FastAPI process. Change-detection logic is developed test-first. Core behavior (chat, rankings, evals) must not change."

## User Scenarios & Testing *(mandatory)*

The users are the same as in feature 001. The **analyst** wants to know, without asking, when a hub's exposure picture changes. The **operator** (the developer or a reviewer) configures where alerts go, triggers checks on demand, and demonstrates the feature.

**Why scores can change at all.** Scores are computed only from data, so a score changes only when the data changes: a new FEMA National Risk Index release, revised weather history, or a change to the hub list or scoring configuration. The historical window is fixed, so on real data changes are rare. This feature therefore watches for change; it does not create change.

### User Story 1 - Get alerted when a hub's score changes (Priority: P1)

On a fixed schedule, the system fetches the latest public data, recomputes every hub's scores with the same deterministic engine as feature 001, and compares them with the last recorded scores. If a hub's score moved by at least the change threshold, the system records an alert and sends it to the configured destination. The alert names the hub, the score that changed, the old and new values, the size of the change, and the data sources and retrieval dates behind the new score.

**Why this priority**: this is the feature. Without detection and delivery, nothing else in this spec has value.

**Independent Test**: start from a recorded set of scores, change the data so one hub's score moves past the threshold, run one check, and verify that exactly one alert is recorded and delivered, with the right hub, old value, new value, and change.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** recorded scores exist, **When** a check finds a hub's score moved by at least the threshold, **Then** one alert is recorded for that hub and score, with old value, new value, and change, all computed by code.
2. **Given** recorded scores exist, **When** a check finds no score moved by at least the threshold, **Then** no alert is recorded and the check itself is still recorded as having run.
3. **Given** no scores have ever been recorded, **When** the first check runs, **Then** it records the scores as the baseline and raises no alerts.
4. **Given** an alert destination is configured, **When** an alert is recorded, **Then** it is delivered to that destination; **Given** none is configured, **Then** the alert is still recorded and listed, and the check reports that delivery was skipped.

---

### User Story 2 - See recent alerts and checks (Priority: P1)

The analyst or operator opens a list of recent alerts, newest first, each showing the hub, the score that changed, old and new values, the change, when it was detected, whether delivery succeeded, and whether it came from a real check or a demonstration. The list is available without the language model.

**Why this priority**: delivery to an external destination can fail or be unconfigured; the recorded list is the reliable record and the main thing a reviewer will look at.

**Independent Test**: after recording alerts, request the list and verify order, fields, and the real/demo label.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** alerts exist, **When** the list is requested, **Then** alerts are returned newest first with all fields above.
2. **Given** no alerts exist, **When** the list is requested, **Then** an empty list is returned along with when the last check ran and how many hubs it covered.
3. **Given** the service restarts, **When** the list is requested, **Then** previously recorded alerts and score history are still there.

---

### User Story 3 - Trigger a check on demand (Priority: P2)

The operator runs a check immediately, instead of waiting for the schedule, from the command line or through the deployed service, and sees a summary: hubs checked, alerts raised, and delivery outcome.

**Delivery**

- **FR-210**: Alerts MUST be sent to a webhook destination taken only from configuration (environment). No API, chat message, or tool may set, read back, or change the destination. Constitution Principle VII.
- **FR-211**: Delivery MUST use a short time limit and a bounded number of attempts. A failed delivery MUST NOT stop the check or affect the rest of the service.
- **FR-212**: Every alert MUST also be written to the service log, whether or not a destination is configured.
- **FR-213**: The delivered message MUST be readable by a person in a common chat tool and also carry the structured alert fields for programs.

**Viewing and triggering**

- **FR-214**: The system MUST provide a list of recent alerts (newest first, bounded size) and the time and summary of the last check, without the language model, at `GET /api/alerts`.
- **FR-215**: The operator MUST be able to trigger a check on demand from the command line and from the deployed service. Triggering through the service MUST require an operator secret from configuration; without a configured secret, triggering through the service MUST be disabled.
- **FR-216**: Only one check MUST run at a time.

**Demonstration**

- **FR-217**: The system MUST provide a demonstration that drives at least one alert through the same detection, recording, delivery, and listing path. Demonstration alerts MUST be labeled as such everywhere they appear, and a demonstration MUST NOT change real scores, real score history used for the next real check, rankings, or chat answers.

**Safety and scope**

- **FR-218**: Chat behavior, rankings, breakdowns, statistics, and the eval results of feature 001 MUST be unchanged. The agent gets no new tools in this feature.
- **FR-219**: Trigger and demonstration requests through the service MUST be rate-limited like chat, so a public URL cannot be used to hammer the public data providers.

### Key Entities

- **Score record**: one hub's watched scores (overall and five hazards) at one check, with the check it belongs to.
- **Check**: one run of the risk-change check: when, scheduled, manual, or demo, outcome, hubs checked, alerts raised, data-fetch failures, data retrieval dates.
- **Alert**: a detected change of one watched score for one hub: old value, new value, difference, detection time, real or demo, delivery status.
- **Alert destination**: a webhook address from configuration; never stored with alerts or exposed through any interface.

## Success Criteria *(mandatory)*

### Measurable Outcomes

- **SC-201**: In tests, for every pair of previous and current scores, the alerts raised equal exactly the watched scores whose change is at least the threshold, with correct old value, new value, and difference (100% on the test set, including the boundary case).
- **SC-202**: A demonstration, run on the deployed service, produces a demo-labeled alert visible in the alert list within 1 minute of triggering, and at the configured destination when one is set.
- **SC-203**: After a restart or redeploy, 100% of previously recorded alerts and score history are still listed.
- **SC-204**: With the destination unreachable, a check still completes, records its alerts as failed deliveries, and chat keeps answering throughout.
- **SC-205**: After this feature ships, all feature-001 tests pass and the eval set still scores 20/20 on the default model.
- **SC-206**: No interface (chat, API, command line output, logs) reveals the configured destination address.

## Assumptions

- **One service instance.** The schedule runs inside the single service process; there is exactly one instance, so only one scheduler runs (Railway does not allow replicas with a volume anyway).
- **Missed runs are not caught up.** If the service is down at a scheduled time, that run is skipped; the next run compares with the last recorded scores, so a change is still caught, only later.
- **Threshold default 2.0 points** on the 0-100 scale: larger than rounding noise (scores are displayed to one decimal), small enough to catch a real data revision. A documented judgment call.
- **Daily default interval.** The underlying data changes at most a few times a year, so checking more often only adds load on free public data providers.
- **Webhook format.** A JSON POST with a human-readable `text` field (accepted by Slack-style incoming webhooks and generic catchers such as webhook.site) plus the structured alert fields.
- **History size.** Kept small and bounded (recent checks and alerts only); long-term retention is out of scope.
- **Out of scope:** alerts on forecasts or live weather events, per-user subscriptions, multiple destinations, email or SMS, alert acknowledgement, and alerts inside the chat page.

lines: -**Feature Branch**: `002-risk-change-alert` (work happens on `main`; no branch hook is configured)

-**Input**: User description: "Risk-change alert (bonus feature). A scheduled job recomputes every hub's risk scores and records them; when a hub's score changes by more than a threshold compared with the last recorded score, the system fires an alert. Alerts go to a webhook URL that comes only from configuration/environment (never from chat), are always logged, and are listed at GET /api/alerts. A manual trigger (CLI command and/or endpoint) runs the check on demand for demos. Because real data changes rarely, there must be a way to demonstrate a change (e.g. a demo command or test fixture). Score history persists across restarts (planned: SQLite on the Railway volume at DATA_DIR). The scheduler runs inside the single FastAPI process. Change-detection logic is developed test-first. Core behavior (chat, rankings, evals) must not change."

-The users are the same as in feature 001. The **analyst** wants to know, without asking, when a hub's exposure picture changes. The **operator** (the developer or a reviewer) configures where alerts go, triggers checks on demand, and demonstrates the feature.

-**Why scores can change at all.** Scores are computed only from data, so a score changes only when the data changes: a new FEMA National Risk Index release, revised weather history, or a change to the hub list or scoring configuration. The historical window is fixed, so on real data changes are rare. This feature therefore watches for change; it does not create change.
-### User Story 1 - Get alerted when a hub's score changes (Priority: P1)

-On a fixed schedule, the system fetches the latest public data, recomputes every hub's scores with the same deterministic engine as feature 001, and compares them with the last recorded scores. If a hub's score moved by at least the change threshold, the system records an alert and sends it to the configured destination. The alert names the hub, the score that changed, the old and new values, the size of the change, and the data sources and retrieval dates behind the new score.
-**Why this priority**: this is the feature. Without detection and delivery, nothing else in this spec has value.

-**Independent Test**: start from a recorded set of scores, change the data so one hub's score moves past the threshold, run one check, and verify that exactly one alert is recorded and delivered, with the right hub, old value, new value, and change.

-1. **Given** recorded scores exist, **When** a check finds a hub's score moved by at least the threshold, **Then** one alert is recorded for that hub and score, with old value, new value, and change, all computed by code.
-2. **Given** recorded scores exist, **When** a check finds no score moved by at least the threshold, **Then** no alert is recorded and the check itself is still recorded as having run.
-3. **Given** no scores have ever been recorded, **When** the first check runs, **Then** it records the scores as the baseline and raises no alerts.

-4. **Given** an alert destination is configured, **When** an alert is recorded, **Then** it is delivered to that destination; **Given** none is configured, **Then** the alert is still recorded and listed, and the check reports that delivery was skipped.
-### User Story 2 - See recent alerts and checks (Priority: P1)

-The analyst or operator opens a list of recent alerts, newest first, each showing the hub, the score that changed, old and new values, the change, when it was detected, whether delivery succeeded, and whether it came from a real check or a demonstration. The list is available without the language model.
-**Why this priority**: delivery to an external destination can fail or be unconfigured; the recorded list is the reliable record and the main thing a reviewer will look at.
-**Independent Test**: after recording alerts, request the list and verify order, fields, and the real/demo label.
-1. **Given** alerts exist, **When** the list is requested, **Then** alerts are returned newest first with all fields above.
-2. **Given** no alerts exist, **When** the list is requested, **Then** an empty list is returned along with when the last check ran and how many hubs it covered.
-3. **Given** the service restarts, **When** the list is requested, **Then** previously recorded alerts and score history are still there.
-### User Story 3 - Trigger a check on demand (Priority: P2)

-The operator runs a check immediately, instead of waiting for the schedule, from the command line or through the deployed service, and sees a summary: hubs checked, alerts raised, and delivery outcome.
-**Why this priority**: needed for demos and for verifying the deployment; the schedule alone makes the feature hard to show.
-**Independent Test**: trigger a check and verify the summary matches what was recorded.
-1. **Given** the operator has the right to trigger checks, **When** a check is triggered, **Then** it runs the same logic as the scheduled check and returns its summary.
-2. **Given** a caller without that right, **When** they try to trigger a check through the deployed service, **Then** the request is refused and nothing runs.
-3. **Given** a check is already running, **When** another is triggered, **Then** the second does not run concurrently; the caller is told a check is in progress.
-### User Story 4 - Demonstrate an alert (Priority: P2)

-Because real data rarely changes, the operator can demonstrate the full path (detect, record, deliver, list) on demand. The demonstration produces a visible score change through the normal detection logic, and every alert it produces is clearly labeled as a demonstration, so it can never be mistaken for a real change.
-**Why this priority**: a reviewer must be able to see the feature work during the interview.
-**Independent Test**: run the demonstration and verify an alert labeled "demo" appears in the list and at the destination, and that real scores, rankings, and chat answers are unchanged afterwards.

-1. **Given** the system is running, **When** the operator runs the demonstration, **Then** at least one alert labeled as a demonstration is recorded, delivered if a destination is configured, and listed.
-2. **Given** a demonstration has run, **When** the analyst asks for rankings or chats, **Then** every score and answer is identical to before the demonstration.
-3. **Given** a demonstration has run, **When** the next real check runs, **Then** it compares against real recorded scores only and raises no alert caused by the demonstration.

-- **Data source down during a scheduled check**: the check uses the existing data for that source (as `refresh` does), records that the fetch failed, and still compares scores; a fetch failure alone never raises a score alert.

-- **Destination down or slow**: delivery is attempted with a short time limit and a bounded number of attempts; the alert stays recorded with delivery marked failed; the check does not crash and the service keeps answering.
-- **Destination returns an error status**: treated as a failed delivery, recorded, not retried forever.
-- **Hub added or removed in the hub list**: a new hub gets a baseline and no alert; a removed hub produces no alert.
-- **Change exactly equal to the threshold**: counts as a change (the rule is "at least the threshold").
-- **Score changes slowly over many checks**: each check compares with the last recorded score, so a slow drift below the threshold per check is not alerted. This is a stated limit.
-- **Service restarts mid-check**: history is never left half-written; the next check compares with the last complete recording.
-- **Chat input mentions webhooks or alerts**: chat has no tool to read or change alert settings or trigger checks; alert configuration is unreachable from chat.
-- **FR-201**: The system MUST run a risk-change check on a fixed schedule while the service is running, with the interval set by configuration (default: once a day).

-- **FR-202**: A check MUST fetch the latest public data the same way the refresh command does, recompute scores with the unchanged feature-001 engine, and record every hub's scores with the time and the data retrieval dates.
-- **FR-203**: The scores watched MUST be each hub's overall score and each of its five hazard scores.

-- **FR-204**: A change MUST be detected when the absolute difference between a watched score and that hub's last recorded value for the same score is at least the change threshold. The threshold MUST be set by configuration, in score points on the 0-100 scale (default: 2.0 points).

-- **FR-205**: Change detection MUST be deterministic plain code: the same previous and current scores always give the same alerts. Old value, new value, and difference MUST be computed by code; no language model is involved anywhere in this feature.
-- **FR-206**: The first check with no recorded history MUST record a baseline and raise no alerts. A hub with no previous record MUST get a baseline, not an alert.
-- **FR-207**: Score history, checks, and alerts MUST persist across service restarts and redeploys, in storage on the persistent volume.
-- **FR-208**: Each check MUST be recorded with start time, outcome, hubs checked, alerts raised, and any data-fetch failures.

-- **FR-209**: Each alert MUST record: hub, score name, old value, new value, difference, detection time, whether it is real or a demonstration, the data retrieval dates behind the new value, and delivery status (delivered, failed with reason, or not configured).

-- **FR-210**: Alerts MUST be sent to a webhook destination taken only from configuration (environment). No API, chat message, or tool may set, read back, or change the destination. Constitution Principle VII.
-- **FR-211**: Delivery MUST use a short time limit and a bounded number of attempts. A failed delivery MUST NOT stop the check or affect the rest of the service.
-- **FR-212**: Every alert MUST also be written to the service log, whether or not a destination is configured.
-- **FR-213**: The delivered message MUST be readable by a person in a common chat tool and also carry the structured alert fields for programs.
-- **FR-214**: The system MUST provide a list of recent alerts (newest first, bounded size) and the time and summary of the last check, without the language model, at `GET /api/alerts`.

-- **FR-215**: The operator MUST be able to trigger a check on demand from the command line and from the deployed service. Triggering through the service MUST require an operator secret from configuration; without a configured secret, triggering through the service MUST be disabled.
-- **FR-216**: Only one check MUST run at a time.

-- **FR-217**: The system MUST provide a demonstration that drives at least one alert through the same detection, recording, delivery, and listing path. Demonstration alerts MUST be labeled as such everywhere they appear, and a demonstration MUST NOT change real scores, real score history used for the next real check, rankings, or chat answers.
-- **FR-218**: Chat behavior, rankings, breakdowns, statistics, and the eval results of feature 001 MUST be unchanged. The agent gets no new tools in this feature.
-- **FR-219**: Trigger and demonstration requests through the service MUST be rate-limited like chat, so a public URL cannot be used to hammer the public data providers.
-- **Score record**: one hub's watched scores (overall and five hazards) at one check, with the check it belongs to.
-- **Check**: one run of the risk-change check: when, scheduled, manual, or demo, outcome, hubs checked, alerts raised, data-fetch failures, data retrieval dates.
-- **Alert**: a detected change of one watched score for one hub: old value, new value, difference, detection time, real or demo, delivery status.
-- **Alert destination**: a webhook address from configuration; never stored with alerts or exposed through any interface.

-- **SC-201**: In tests, for every pair of previous and current scores, the alerts raised equal exactly the watched scores whose change is at least the threshold, with correct old value, new value, and difference (100% on the test set, including the boundary case).
-- **SC-202**: A demonstration, run on the deployed service, produces a demo-labeled alert visible in the alert list within 1 minute of triggering, and at the configured destination when one is set.
-- **SC-203**: After a restart or redeploy, 100% of previously recorded alerts and score history are still listed.
-- **SC-204**: With the destination unreachable, a check still completes, records its alerts as failed deliveries, and chat keeps answering throughout.
-- **SC-205**: After this feature ships, all feature-001 tests pass and the eval set still scores 20/20 on the default model.
-- **SC-206**: No interface (chat, API, command line output, logs) reveals the configured destination address.
-- **One service instance.** The schedule runs inside the single service process; there is exactly one instance, so only one scheduler runs (Railway does not allow replicas with a volume anyway).
-- **Missed runs are not caught up.** If the service is down at a scheduled time, that run is skipped; the next run compares with the last recorded scores, so a change is still caught, only later.
-- **Threshold default 2.0 points** on the 0-100 scale: larger than rounding noise (scores are displayed to one decimal), small enough to catch a real data revision. A documented judgment call.
-- **Daily default interval.** The underlying data changes at most a few times a year, so checking more often only adds load on free public data providers.
-- **Webhook format.** A JSON POST with a human-readable `text` field (accepted by Slack-style incoming webhooks and generic catchers such as webhook.site) plus the structured alert fields.
-- **History size.** Kept small and bounded (recent checks and alerts only); long-term retention is out of scope.
-- **Out of scope:** alerts on forecasts or live weather events, per-user subscriptions, multiple destinations, email or SMS, alert acknowledgement, and alerts inside the chat page.

+- **History size.** Kept small and bounded (recent checks and alerts only); long-term retention is out of scope.
+- **Out of scope:** alerts on forecasts or live weather events, per-user subscriptions, multiple destinations, email or SMS, alert acknowledgement, and alerts inside the chat page.

content.text:
The spec and clarifications are committed as `a70afaf`.

- **Files:** `specs/002-risk-change-alert/spec.md`, plus `checklists/requirements.md` (16/16 passing, no regressions).
- **Clarifications:** 4 questions asked and answered. They touched the Clarifications section, FR-202, FR-215, FR-217, FR-218 and User Story 3.

**What the spec says, in short:**
- **Schedule:** a check runs daily by default. It works like `wra refresh`: it fetches live data into `DATA_DIR`, so the alerts and the chat always describe the same data. It never touches the committed seed.
- **Detection:** it then recomputes scores with the unchanged engine. An alert fires when a hub's overall score or any of its 5 hazard scores moves by **≥ 2.0 points** against the last recorded value. The first check only records a baseline. Detection is plain code, and no LLM is involved anywhere in this feature.
- **Records:** score history, checks and alerts persist on the volume. Every alert is logged and listed at public `GET /api/alerts`.
- **Delivery:** alerts go to a webhook URL that comes only from env. They are sent with a short timeout and bounded retries, and a failed delivery is recorded rather than crashing anything.
- **Manual trigger and demo:** both are available from the CLI with no token. On the service, both need the `ALERT_ADMIN_TOKEN` bearer token, and with no token configured they are disabled.
- **How the demo works:** it compares today's real scores against a *simulated previous* copy, shifted for one or two hubs. Its alerts are labeled "demo", and it never writes to the real history.

**Coverage:**

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| Scope, demo, change rule, trigger security, data flow | Resolved |
| Failure handling, persistence, Principle VII (webhook from config only) | Clear |
| Retry count, history size, scheduler mechanism (in-app loop vs APScheduler), SQLite schema | Deferred to the plan (implementation details) |

**Do you approve the spec?** If you do, I'll run `speckit-plan`, where I'll grill you on the scheduler mechanism and the storage design, and then bring you the plan for approval.

# Implementation Plan: Core Weather Risk Agent

**Branch**: `001-core-risk-agent` | **Date**: 2026-11-13 | **Spec**: [spec.md](spec.md)

**Input**: Feature specification from `/specs/001-core-risk-agent/spec.md`

## Summary

Build a deterministic weather-exposure engine for 16 US hubs, with a conversational agent on top. The engine combines two public, keyless sources: FEMA National Risk Index county event frequencies, as national percentiles, and 10 years of Open-Meteo ERA5 daily weather, as fixed-scale indicators. It produces five hazard scores and an overall score per hub, each a transparent weighted sum. The scores, rankings, breakdowns, and statistics are plain Python, available without any LLM through a CLI and API endpoints.

An OpenAI agent, built as a hand-written Responses API loop with five strict, read-only tools, answers ranking, "why", comparison, statistic, and follow-up questions. Its final answer is a strict JSON schema (narrative, assumptions, limitations, confidence). Code renders all numbers and attaches the data sources. FastAPI serves the API and a one-file chat page. A YAML eval set of about 20 cases runs with `wra eval`, using deterministic checks.

## Technical Context

**Language/Version**: Python 3.12

**Primary Dependencies**: FastAPI, Uvicorn, `openai` SDK (Responses API), Pydantic v2, pydantic-settings, httpx, Typer, PyYAML. Dev: pytest, ruff.

**Storage**: JSON files. The committed seed snapshot is in `data/seed/`. Refreshed data goes to `DATA_DIR`, which is a Railway volume in production. Everything else lives in memory. No database in this feature (see Complexity Tracking).

**Testing**: pytest. Unit tests are written test-first for indicators, percentiles, scoring, ranking, and statistics. Smoke tests cover the API and CLI. Agent behavior is covered by the evals.

**Target Platform**: local Windows or Linux development; Railway (Linux container) for deployment, which comes after this feature's core.

**Project Type**: web service with a CLI (single Python package)

**Performance Goals**: chat answers within 30 seconds for 95% of questions (SC-008). LLM-free endpoints under 1 second.

**Constraints**: works offline from the data providers using the seed (SC-007). Open-Meteo non-commercial terms. At most 6 model calls per user message. Input limited to 1,000 characters.

**Scale/Scope**: 16 hubs, 5 hazards, 10 years of daily data (about 58,000 hub-days), about 3,232 NRI counties. Single-tenant demo.

All unknowns were resolved in [research.md](research.md); none remain.

## Constitution Check

*GATE: Must pass before Phase 0 research. Re-check after Phase 1 design.*

| Principle | How this plan complies | Status |
|---|---|---|
| I. Deterministic scoring, LLM explains | All scores, ranks, and statistics are pure functions in `scoring/`. Tools return engine output, code renders tables, and the LLM writes only the narrative. Each score is a weighted sum with its components returned (data-model §4-5). The same functions back the CLI, the API, and the tools (FR-029). | Pass |
| II. Enforced structured contracts | Strict function tools plus a strict `text.format` JSON schema generated from Pydantic, re-validated with Pydantic, one retry, then an error. All LLM calls go through one module, `agent/llm.py`. | Pass |
| III. Grounded and honest | `AgentAnswer` requires assumptions, limitations, and confidence. Code attaches `data_sources` with periods. Unknown hubs and hazards are impossible to express in the tool enums, so the agent must use `list_coverage` and say so. | Pass |
| IV. Test-first and evals | TDD for `scoring/` and `data/` parsing. About 20 eval cases across 8 categories, run with `wra eval`. Primary checks are deterministic, including numbers matching the engine. | Pass, with one adaptation (see Complexity Tracking) |
| V. Narrow scope, explainable code | No agent framework, a loop of about 80 lines, one package, no frontend build. Alerts and voice are left to their own specs. | Pass |
| VI. Reproducible public data | Keyless public sources. A committed seed snapshot. Hubs in one config file. Atomic per-source refresh. | Pass |
| VII. Safe by default | Key from the environment, `.env` git-ignored, an allow-list of 5 read-only tools, enum-typed arguments, a length limit, and a step limit. No outbound calls are triggered by chat. | Pass |

**Post-design re-check (after Phase 1)**: still passes. The data model keeps every score decomposable (`sum(contributions) == score` is a tested rule). The contracts keep numbers out of the LLM's output (`AgentAnswer` has no numeric fields).

## Project Structure

### Documentation (this feature)

```text
specs/001-core-risk-agent/
├── plan.md              # This file
├── research.md          # Phase 0: sources, scoring method, model, storage
├── data-model.md        # Phase 1: entities, indicators, weights, statistics
├── quickstart.md        # Phase 1: run and validation guide
├── contracts/
│   ├── http-api.md      # REST endpoints
│   ├── agent-tools.md   # 5 tools, answer schema, loop rules
│   └── cli.md           # wra commands
└── tasks.md             # Phase 2 (/speckit-tasks)
```

### Source Code (repository root)

```text
config/
└── hubs.toml                  # 16 hubs, state→region map
data/
└── seed/                      # committed real API responses
    ├── manifest.json          # retrieval dates, NRI version, window
    ├── nri_counties.json      # all counties, AFREQ columns only
    └── weather/<hub_id>.json  # 16 files, daily ERA5 2016-2025
src/weather_risk/
├── settings.py                # env config (OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_MODEL, DATA_DIR)
├── hubs.py                    # load hubs and regions
├── data/
│   ├── models.py              # DailyWeather, WeatherDataset, NriCounty, NriDataset
│   ├── sources.py             # Open-Meteo and FEMA NRI fetchers (refresh only)
│   └── store.py               # load newest snapshot; atomic write
├── scoring/
│   ├── indicators.py          # FEMA percentiles, observed day counts → 0-100
│   ├── engine.py              # hazard + overall scores, ranking, breakdown, compare
│   └── stats.py               # weather statistics
├── agent/
│   ├── schemas.py             # tool argument models, AgentAnswer, ChatResponse
│   ├── tools.py               # 5 tools: call engine, build display tables + sources
│   ├── prompts.py             # system prompt
│   ├── llm.py                 # the only module that talks to OpenAI
│   └── loop.py                # tool-calling loop, validation, retry, step limit
├── api/
│   ├── app.py                 # FastAPI app, routes, conversation store
│   └── static/index.html      # chat page (HTML + inline JS)
└── cli.py                     # wra rank | breakdown | stat | refresh | eval | serve
evals/
├── cases.yaml                 # ~20 cases, 8 categories
├── run.py                     # runner + deterministic checks + report
└── results/                   # timestamped JSON results (committed for submission)
tests/
├── unit/                      # indicators, percentiles, engine, stats, schemas
└── smoke/                     # API routes, CLI commands
docs/
├── decisions.md               # decision log (exists)
└── architecture.md            # design doc deliverable (written at the end)
pyproject.toml, uv.lock, .env.example, README.md
```

**Structure Decision**: a single Python package, `src/weather_risk`, with four layers that only call downward: `api`/`cli` → `agent` → `scoring` → `data`. The scoring layer never imports the agent, which keeps the deterministic engine independent of the LLM. That independence is the point of FR-029.

## Build order (input to /speckit-tasks)

1. Project skeleton (uv, settings, hubs config) and the seed snapshot fetch (`wra refresh` writes `data/seed` once).
2. Scoring engine test-first: indicators, percentiles, hazard scores, overall, ranking with tie-break, breakdown, compare, statistics.
3. LLM-free surfaces: `wra rank|breakdown|stat`, `GET /api/rankings`, `GET /api/hubs/{id}/breakdown` (JSON, browsable at `/docs`), plus the plausibility tests from data-model §5. This is a demonstrable milestone even if the agent slips.
4. Agent: schemas, tools, the LLM module, the loop, the system prompt; `POST /api/chat` with conversation memory.
5. Chat page.
6. Eval set and runner; iterate on the prompt until at least 90% pass.
7. README and architecture doc (deployment to Railway follows as its own small step).

## Complexity Tracking

| Deviation | Why needed | Simpler alternative rejected because |
|---|---|---|
| JSON files instead of SQLite (constitution: "SQLite unless a plan justifies otherwise") | The seed must be plain files in git anyway, and this feature has no queries, history, or concurrent writers. JSON files are simpler. | Adding SQLite now adds a schema and a loader for no benefit. It arrives with spec 002, where score history needs it. |
| ~~`reasoning_effort` instead of "low temperature"~~ Resolved by constitution v1.1.1, which now says "lowest-variance settings the model supports". | n/a | n/a |

"""HTTP API (contracts/http-api.md). One FastAPI process serves the API and the chat page.

The LLM-free endpoints (/api/rankings, /api/hubs/{id}/breakdown) read the same engine the
agent's tools use, so the numbers are identical on every path (FR-029).
"""

import threading
from pathlib import Path

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Query, Request
from fastapi.responses import FileResponse, JSONResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator

from weather_risk.agent.conversations import ConversationStore

from weather_risk.settings import get_settings

app = FastAPI(title="Weather Risk Intelligence Agent", version="0.1.0")


class EngineHolder:
    """Builds the engine once and rebuilds it when a refresh rewrites a manifest (FR-008)."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._engine: Engine | None = None
        self._version = -1.0
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def get(self) -> Engine:
        s = get_settings()
        version = snapshot_version(s.seed_dir, s.data_dir)
        with self._lock:
            if self._engine is None or version != self._version:
                self._engine = Engine.from_settings()
                self._version = version
            return self._engine

content.text: Before writing the plan, I need four design decisions from you. They are the ones you flagged as "to confirm", plus one that came up while reading the code.

questions.question: How should the scheduler run inside the FastAPI process?

options.label: asyncio loop in lifespan (Recommended)
options.description: ~25 lines, no new dependency: a background task started in FastAPI's lifespan wakes every few minutes, asks SQLite 'is a check due?' (last check + interval), and runs it in a worker thread. Because 'due' is computed from the DB, redeploys neither skip nor repeat checks. Fully explainable.

options.label: APScheduler
options.description: Add APScheduler (BackgroundScheduler, interval or cron trigger). Familiar, cron syntax, misfire handling built in, but a new dependency and its job state lives in memory unless you add its job store; schedule restarts from zero on each redeploy.

questions.question: How should score history, checks and alerts be stored on the volume?

options.label: sqlite3 stdlib, raw SQL (Recommended)
options.description: One file DATA_DIR/alerts.sqlite, 3 tables (checks, score_records, alerts), ~10 short SQL statements in one module. No ORM, no migrations tool; schema created with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS. Matches the constitution (SQLite arrives with this feature).

options.label: SQLModel / SQLAlchemy
options.description: Typed models and a session layer. Nicer for growth, but a new dependency and more to explain for 3 tables.

options.label: JSON-lines files
options.description: Append-only checks.jsonl and alerts.jsonl. Simplest, but needs a constitution justification and hand-rolled 'last value per hub' lookups.

questions.question: Which webhook destination will you use for the live demo? The payload format depends on it.

options.label: webhook.site (Recommended)
options.description: Free throwaway URL, shows every POST with headers and JSON in the browser; nothing to set up. Payload: {text, alert fields}. Also works with Slack incoming webhooks unchanged.

options.label: Slack incoming webhook
options.description: Real chat message in a Slack channel you own. Payload {text, ...}; Slack ignores the extra fields.

options.label: Discord webhook
options.description: Discord needs a `content` field instead of `text`; I'd send both fields so either works.

questions.question: How should alerts treat score precision? Scores are shown to one decimal.

options.label: Compare displayed values (Recommended)
options.description: Store and compare scores rounded to 1 decimal, exactly as users see them, so an alert's old/new/change always match the numbers in rankings and chat. A raw 1.96 move displayed as 30.0 to 32.0 alerts, consistently with what is shown.

options.label: Compare raw values
options.description: Store full precision and compare unrounded. Mathematically exact, but an alert can show a displayed change of 2.0 that did not fire, or the reverse, which is hard to explain to an analyst.

# Implementation Plan: Risk-Change Alert

**Branch**: `002-risk-change-alert` (work on `main`) | **Date**: 2026-11-13 | **Spec**: [spec.md](spec.md)

**Input**: Feature specification from `/specs/002-risk-change-alert/spec.md`

## Summary

Add a risk-change check that runs on a schedule inside the existing FastAPI process. A check does the same fetch as `wra refresh` into `DATA_DIR`. It then recomputes scores with the unchanged engine, rounds each hub's overall and five hazard scores to one decimal (as displayed), and compares them with the last recorded real check. Every change of at least 2.0 points becomes an alert.

- **Storage:** checks, score records and alerts go into one SQLite file on the volume (stdlib `sqlite3`, raw SQL).
- **Delivery:** each alert is logged and POSTed to a webhook URL that comes only from env.
- **Viewing:** alerts are listed at public `GET /api/alerts`.
- **Manual trigger:** `wra alerts check|demo|list` from the CLI, or token-protected `POST /api/alerts/check|demo` on the service.
- **Demo:** it compares today's real scores with a simulated previous set (fixed shifts for two hubs), and stores its alerts labeled `demo` without writing score history.
- **Test-first:** change detection is a pure function, developed test-first.

## Technical Context

**Language/Version**: Python 3.12

**Primary Dependencies**: unchanged (FastAPI, httpx, Typer, Pydantic). New: stdlib `sqlite3`, `asyncio`, `hmac`, `logging` only. No new packages.

**Storage**: SQLite file `DATA_DIR/alerts.sqlite` (Railway volume at `/data`). The JSON snapshot files from 001 are unchanged.

**Testing**: pytest. Test-first for `alerts/detect.py` (detection, rounding, boundary, baseline, new and removed hubs, demo shifts) and for the history queries (last real scores ignore demo checks, persistence across reopen). Smoke tests for the endpoints (auth, 409 busy, list), webhook delivery against a fake transport, CLI commands, and the scheduler's "is a check due" rule.

**Target Platform**: Railway, one container, one instance, volume at `/data`. Local Windows for development.

**Project Type**: web service with a CLI (existing single package).

**Performance Goals**: a demo appears in the list within 1 minute (SC-202). A real check takes about 1 minute, because the Open-Meteo fetch pauses 3 s between hubs, and it runs in a worker thread so chat is never blocked.

**Constraints**:
- The webhook URL never appears in any response, log line, or error message (SC-206).
- Delivery: 5 s timeout, at most 3 attempts.
- Only one check at a time.
- The scheduler is off unless `ALERT_INTERVAL_HOURS > 0`, so local `wra serve` and the evals never fetch live data by surprise.

**Scale/Scope**: 16 hubs × 6 scores = 96 values per check. Score records are kept for the last 30 real checks; the alert list returns the newest 50.

No unknowns remain; the decisions are in [research.md](research.md).

## Constitution Check

*GATE: Must pass before Phase 0 research. Re-check after Phase 1 design.*

| Principle | How this plan complies | Status |
|---|---|---|
| I. Deterministic scoring, LLM explains | Scores come from the unchanged 001 engine. Detection is a pure function. Old value, new value and change are computed by code. No LLM anywhere in this feature. | Pass |
| II. Enforced structured contracts | No LLM output is consumed. The webhook payload and API responses are Pydantic models. | Pass (n/a for LLM) |
| III. Grounded and honest | Every alert carries the data retrieval dates. Demo alerts are labeled `demo` in the DB, the API, the webhook text and the logs. Known limit (slow drift under the threshold) is in the spec and README. | Pass |
| IV. Test-first and evals | TDD for detection and history queries; smoke tests for routes, CLI and scheduler (the constitution's scope). The eval set is rerun at the end: 20/20 expected, since chat is untouched. | Pass |
| V. Narrow scope, explainable code | No scheduler library and no ORM: an asyncio loop of about 25 lines and about 10 SQL statements. The agent gets no new tools. | Pass |
| VI. Reproducible public data | The check reuses the refresh fetch and its atomic per-source writes. The seed is never modified. Same inputs give the same alerts. | Pass |
| VII. Safe by default | Webhook URL and admin token only from env. Token compared with `hmac.compare_digest`. Trigger endpoints are disabled when no token is set, and rate-limited. The only write is the alert job's own store, which this principle explicitly allows. | Pass |

**Post-design re-check (after Phase 1)**: still passes.
- The data model keeps demo checks out of "last real scores" through a SQL `WHERE kind != 'demo'`, which is covered by a test.
- The contracts never return the webhook URL; `/api/alerts` shows only `webhook_configured: true|false`.

## Project Structure

### Documentation (this feature)

```text
specs/002-risk-change-alert/
├── plan.md              # This file
├── research.md          # Phase 0: scheduler, storage, precision, delivery, demo, auth
├── data-model.md        # Phase 1: tables, detection rule, demo shifts
├── quickstart.md        # Phase 1: run and validation guide
├── contracts/
│   ├── http-api.md      # GET /api/alerts, POST /api/alerts/check, POST /api/alerts/demo
│   ├── cli.md           # wra alerts check | demo | list
│   └── webhook.md       # payload sent to the destination
└── tasks.md             # Phase 2 (/speckit-tasks)
```

### Source Code (repository root)

```text
src/weather_risk/
├── settings.py              # + alert_interval_hours, alert_threshold, alert_webhook_url,
│                            #   alert_admin_token
├── data/
│   └── refresh.py           # NEW: fetch loop moved out of cli.py, shared by refresh and checks
├── alerts/                  # NEW package
│   ├── detect.py            # pure: watched_scores(engine), detect_changes(), simulate_previous()
│   ├── history.py           # sqlite3: schema, last_real_scores, record_check, list_alerts, due
│   ├── notify.py            # webhook payload + POST with timeout/retries; logs every alert
│   ├── service.py           # run_check(kind) / run_demo(): orchestration + one-at-a-time lock
│   └── scheduler.py         # asyncio loop: every 10 min, run a check in a thread if due
├── api/app.py               # + lifespan starts the scheduler; + 3 alert routes
└── cli.py                   # refresh uses data/refresh.py; + `wra alerts check|demo|list`
tests/
├── unit/test_alert_detect.py, test_alert_history.py, test_alert_notify.py
└── smoke/test_api_alerts.py, test_cli_alerts.py, test_scheduler.py
```

**Structure Decision**:
- **Dependencies point downward:** `alerts` depends on `scoring` and `data`; `api` and `cli` depend on `alerts`. Nothing in `scoring` or `agent` imports `alerts`.
- **Chat is unchanged:** the agent cannot reach alerts (FR-218, Principle VII).
- **Refresh is shared:** the fetch loop moves from `cli.py` to `data/refresh.py`, so `wra refresh` and a check fetch data the same way (FR-202).

## Build order (input to /speckit-tasks)

1. Extract `data/refresh.py` from `cli.py`, with behavior unchanged and the existing tests green.
2. `alerts/detect.py`, test-first.
3. `alerts/history.py`, test-first.
4. `alerts/notify.py`: payload and delivery, with a fake transport in tests.
5. `alerts/service.py`: run_check and run_demo, plus the CLI `wra alerts ...`.
6. API routes plus the lifespan scheduler, with smoke tests.
7. Full tests and `wra eval` (20/20 expected), then docs.

## Complexity Tracking

No constitution deviations. One design note: the trigger endpoints add an operator token, the first credential the app checks itself. It is a single shared secret from env, compared in constant time; there are no user accounts, which is in line with the single-tenant demo assumption.

# Research: Risk-Change Alert

Each decision was confirmed by the user on 2026-11-13. The spec-level choices are in [spec.md](spec.md) under Clarifications; these are the plan-level ones.

## 1. Scheduler: asyncio loop in the FastAPI lifespan

- **Decision:** the FastAPI `lifespan` starts one asyncio task. Every 10 minutes it asks the history store whether a check is due (`now >= last real check start + ALERT_INTERVAL_HOURS`, or no check yet). If one is due, it runs the check with `asyncio.to_thread`, because the fetch is blocking httpx with 3 s pauses. The task is cancelled on shutdown.
- **Rationale:** about 25 lines, no dependency. Because "due" is computed from SQLite, a redeploy neither skips nor repeats a check. A 10-minute poll is ample for a daily job.
- **Off by default:** `ALERT_INTERVAL_HOURS=0` disables it, so local `wra serve` and test clients never fetch live data or move `data/live`, and evals stay on the seed. Railway sets `ALERT_INTERVAL_HOURS=24`.
- **Alternatives:** APScheduler, a dependency whose in-memory schedule restarts from zero on each redeploy unless you add its job store; Railway cron, a second service with no shared process or volume.

## 2. Storage: stdlib sqlite3 with raw SQL

- **Decision:** one file, `DATA_DIR/alerts.sqlite`, with 3 tables (see [data-model.md](data-model.md)), created with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`. A new connection per operation, so it is thread-safe across the scheduler thread and request threads. Each check, with its score records and alerts, is written in one transaction (spec edge case: no half-written history).
- **Rationale:** the constitution names SQLite for score history; 3 small tables do not need an ORM.
- **Alternatives:** SQLModel or SQLAlchemy (a dependency, more to explain); JSON-lines files (needs a constitution justification and hand-written lookups).

## 3. Precision: compare displayed values

- **Decision:** watched scores are rounded to one decimal, as every surface displays them, before they are stored and compared. `change = round(new - old, 1)`, and an alert fires when `abs(change) >= threshold`.
- **Rationale:** an alert's old value, new value and change always match what rankings and chat show. The boundary case (a change of exactly 2.0) is exact after rounding.
- **Alternative:** compare raw floats. A displayed change of 2.0 could then fail to fire, or a displayed 1.9 could fire.

## 4. Delivery: generic JSON webhook, tested with webhook.site

- **Decision:** one POST per alert. The body has a human-readable `text` (Slack-compatible) plus the structured fields ([contracts/webhook.md](contracts/webhook.md)). 5 s timeout and up to 3 attempts with 1 s and 2 s waits. Any non-2xx response or exception counts as a failure, and the status and reason are stored. Every alert is also logged at WARNING with the `text`. The URL is never logged; errors are stored as an exception class name or HTTP status only.
- **Rationale:** webhook.site shows each POST live for the demo, and Slack works unchanged.

## 5. Demo: simulated previous scores

- **Decision:** `simulate_previous(current)` returns a copy of today's real watched scores with two fixed shifts: Dallas `heat` 7.5 lower and Miami `hurricane` 5.0 higher. Detection, recording, delivery and listing then run as normal. The result is exactly 2 alerts: Dallas heat up 7.5, Miami hurricane down 5.0. Overall scores are untouched, which also shows that sub-threshold scores do not alert. The demo check row has `kind='demo'`, its alerts have `is_demo=1`, and no score records are written.
- **Rationale:** it exercises the real code path, cannot affect the next real check, and its output is predictable for a live demo.

## 6. Trigger protection: operator bearer token

- **Decision:** `POST /api/alerts/check` and `/api/alerts/demo` require `Authorization: Bearer <ALERT_ADMIN_TOKEN>`, compared with `hmac.compare_digest`. With no token configured they return 403. They have their own rate limiter (2 per minute, 50 per day). A busy check returns 409. `GET /api/alerts` is public and returns `webhook_configured`, never the URL.
- **Rationale:** the URL is public, and a real check makes 17 calls to free public APIs.

## 7. Refresh reuse

- **Decision:** move the fetch loop from `cli.refresh` to `data/refresh.py` (`fetch_all(root, source) -> RefreshResult` with the failures and per-source results). `wra refresh` keeps its output and exit codes; a check calls the same function on `DATA_DIR` and then `mark_refresh_complete`, so the server's engine reloads (the 001 mechanism).
- **Rationale:** FR-202 says "the same way the refresh command does"; one function guarantees it.

## 8. Concurrency

- **Decision:** a module-level `threading.Lock` in `alerts/service.py`, taken with `acquire(blocking=False)`. If it is busy, the API returns 409 and the scheduler skips that tick.
- **Known limit:** a `wra alerts check` started from a second process at the same moment is not covered by the lock. SQLite transactions keep the history consistent and refresh writes are atomic, so the worst case is two baseline-equivalent checks. Documented, not engineered around.

# Data Model: Risk-Change Alert

All tables live in `DATA_DIR/alerts.sqlite`. Times are UTC ISO-8601 strings (`2026-11-13T18:00:00Z`).

## 1. Watched scores

`watched_scores(engine) -> dict[hub_id, dict[metric, float]]`, where `metric` is one of `overall, winter, hurricane, flood, heat, severe_storms` (the 001 `METRICS`). The values are `round(engine.metric_score(hub, metric), 1)`. That gives 16 × 6 = 96 values.

## 2. Detection rule (pure, test-first)

`detect_changes(previous, current, threshold) -> list[Change]`

- For every hub in **both** `previous` and `current`, and every metric in both: `change = round(current - previous, 1)`. Emit `Change(hub_id, metric, old, new, change)` when `abs(change) >= threshold`.
- A hub only in `current` (new hub) gives no change; it becomes part of the baseline. A hub only in `previous` (removed hub) gives no change.
- `previous` empty (first check) gives `[]`; the check is marked `baseline=1`.
- Output order is sorted by `(hub_id, metric)`, so it is deterministic.
- Validation: `threshold > 0`.

`simulate_previous(current) -> previous`: a deep copy with `dallas.heat -= 7.5` and `miami.hurricane += 5.0` (rounded to 1 decimal), giving exactly 2 changes at the default threshold of 2.0. If a hub or metric is missing, that shift is skipped.

## 3. Tables

### `checks`

| Column | Type | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| id | INTEGER PK | autoincrement |
| kind | TEXT | `scheduled`, `manual`, or `demo` |
| started_at, finished_at | TEXT | UTC ISO |
| status | TEXT | `ok` or `failed` (a failure inside the check itself, e.g. scoring error) |
| baseline | INTEGER | 1 if there was no previous real check |
| hubs_checked | INTEGER | |
| alerts_raised | INTEGER | |
| fetch_failures | TEXT | JSON list of `"weather:dallas"`, `"nri"`; empty for demo |
| data_retrieved | TEXT | JSON of the engine's `data_sources()` after the fetch |

### `score_records` (real checks only, never demo)

| Column | Type | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| check_id | INTEGER FK → checks.id | |
| hub_id, metric | TEXT | |
| value | REAL | one decimal |
| | | PK (check_id, hub_id, metric) |

**Last real scores:** the records of `MAX(id) FROM checks WHERE kind != 'demo' AND status = 'ok'`.

**Retention:** after each real check, delete the records of checks older than the newest 30 real checks.

### `alerts`

| Column | Type | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| id | INTEGER PK | |
| check_id | INTEGER FK | |
| hub_id, metric | TEXT | |
| old_value, new_value, change | REAL | from `detect_changes` |
| detected_at | TEXT | the check's `started_at` |
| is_demo | INTEGER | 1 for demo |
| data_retrieved | TEXT | JSON copy from the check |
| delivery_status | TEXT | `delivered`, `failed`, or `not_configured` |
| delivery_error | TEXT NULL | e.g. `HTTP 500`, `ConnectTimeout`; never the URL |

## 4. Lifecycle of one check

1. Take the lock, or return busy.
2. Real check: `fetch_all(DATA_DIR)`, mark the refresh complete, and build the engine. Demo: build the engine from current data, with no fetch.
3. `current = watched_scores(engine)`. `previous` = the last real scores (real check), or `simulate_previous(current)` (demo).
4. `changes = detect_changes(previous, current, threshold)`.
5. In one transaction: insert the check row, the score records (real only) and the alert rows with `delivery_status='not_configured'` or `'pending'`. Then prune.
6. Outside the transaction: for each alert, log it, deliver it if a URL is configured, and update `delivery_status` and `delivery_error`.
7. Release the lock and return a summary (see the contracts).

A failure in step 2 for one source is recorded in `fetch_failures`, and the old data is kept. If scoring itself fails, the check is recorded as `failed` with no score records, so the next check compares with the last good one.

# Research: Risk-Change Alert

Each decision was confirmed by the user on 2026-11-13. The spec-level choices are in [spec.md](spec.md) under Clarifications; these are the plan-level ones.

## 1. Scheduler: asyncio loop in the FastAPI lifespan

- **Decision:** the FastAPI `lifespan` starts one asyncio task. Every 10 minutes it asks the history store whether a check is due (`now >= last real check start + ALERT_INTERVAL_HOURS`, or no check yet). If one is due, it runs the check with `asyncio.to_thread`, because the fetch is blocking httpx with 3 s pauses. The task is cancelled on shutdown.
- **Rationale:** about 25 lines, no dependency. Because "due" is computed from SQLite, a redeploy neither skips nor repeats a check. A 10-minute poll is ample for a daily job.
- **Off by default:** `ALERT_INTERVAL_HOURS=0` disables it, so local `wra serve` and test clients never fetch live data or move `data/live`, and evals stay on the seed. Railway sets `ALERT_INTERVAL_HOURS=24`.
- **Alternatives:** APScheduler, a dependency whose in-memory schedule restarts from zero on each redeploy unless you add its job store; Railway cron, a second service with no shared process or volume.

## 2. Storage: stdlib sqlite3 with raw SQL

- **Decision:** one file, `DATA_DIR/alerts.sqlite`, with 3 tables (see [data-model.md](data-model.md)), created with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`. A new connection per operation, so it is thread-safe across the scheduler thread and request threads. Each check, with its score records and alerts, is written in one transaction (spec edge case: no half-written history).
- **Rationale:** the constitution names SQLite for score history; 3 small tables do not need an ORM.
- **Alternatives:** SQLModel or SQLAlchemy (a dependency, more to explain); JSON-lines files (needs a constitution justification and hand-written lookups).

## 3. Precision: compare displayed values

- **Decision:** watched scores are rounded to one decimal, as every surface displays them, before they are stored and compared. `change = round(new - old, 1)`, and an alert fires when `abs(change) >= threshold`.
- **Rationale:** an alert's old value, new value and change always match what rankings and chat show. The boundary case (a change of exactly 2.0) is exact after rounding.
- **Alternative:** compare raw floats. A displayed change of 2.0 could then fail to fire, or a displayed 1.9 could fire.

## 4. Delivery: generic JSON webhook, tested with webhook.site

- **Decision:** one POST per alert. The body has a human-readable `text` (Slack-compatible) plus the structured fields ([contracts/webhook.md](contracts/webhook.md)). 5 s timeout and up to 3 attempts with 1 s and 2 s waits. Any non-2xx response or exception counts as a failure, and the status and reason are stored. Every alert is also logged at WARNING with the `text`. The URL is never logged; errors are stored as an exception class name or HTTP status only.
- **Rationale:** webhook.site shows each POST live for the demo, and Slack works unchanged.

## 5. Demo: simulated previous scores

- **Decision:** `simulate_previous(current)` returns a copy of today's real watched scores with two fixed shifts: Dallas `heat` 7.5 lower and Miami `hurricane` 5.0 higher. Detection, recording, delivery and listing then run as normal. The result is exactly 2 alerts: Dallas heat up 7.5, Miami hurricane down 5.0. Overall scores are untouched, which also shows that sub-threshold scores do not alert. The demo check row has `kind='demo'`, its alerts have `is_demo=1`, and no score records are written.
- **Rationale:** it exercises the real code path, cannot affect the next real check, and its output is predictable for a live demo.

## 6. Trigger protection: operator bearer token

- **Decision:** `POST /api/alerts/check` and `/api/alerts/demo` require `Authorization: Bearer <ALERT_ADMIN_TOKEN>`, compared with `hmac.compare_digest`. With no token configured they return 403. They have their own rate limiter (2 per minute, 50 per day). A busy check returns 409. `GET /api/alerts` is public and returns `webhook_configured`, never the URL.
- **Rationale:** the URL is public, and a real check makes 17 calls to free public APIs.

## 7. Refresh reuse

- **Decision:** move the fetch loop from `cli.refresh` to `data/refresh.py` (`fetch_all(root, source) -> RefreshResult` with the failures and per-source results). `wra refresh` keeps its output and exit codes; a check calls the same function on `DATA_DIR` and then `mark_refresh_complete`, so the server's engine reloads (the 001 mechanism).
- **Rationale:** FR-202 says "the same way the refresh command does"; one function guarantees it.

## 8. Concurrency

- **Decision:** a module-level `threading.Lock` in `alerts/service.py`, taken with `acquire(blocking=False)`. If it is busy, the API returns 409 and the scheduler skips that tick.
- **Known limit:** a `wra alerts check` started from a second process at the same moment is not covered by the lock. SQLite transactions keep the history consistent and refresh writes are atomic, so the worst case is two baseline-equivalent checks. Documented, not engineered around.
